classification.difficultyReason: Derives the general area scale-factor relationship from a similarity proof and corresponding altitudes.

content.prompt:
Suppose that the scale factor between two similar triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ is $k$. That is:
$$\frac{DE}{AB}=\frac{EF}{BC}=\frac{FD}{CA}=k.$$
Draw altitudes through a pair of corresponding vertices of the triangles.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 12, paired triangles in the upper left column
spec.description: Corresponding triangles remain paired horizontally. Source yellow interior shading is omitted because it conveys no additional mathematical information.
spec.mathematics: Similar triangles ABC and DEF; A,X,C and D,Y,F are collinear; BX and EY are perpendicular altitudes with feet inside their bases. Drawing coordinates are illustrative, not numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: All triangles, altitudes, vertex labels and right-angle marks are permanent supplied content.

answer.short: $\angle BAX=\angle EDY$ and $\angle AXB=\angle DYE=90^\circ$. Therefore, $\triangle ABX\sim\triangle DEY$ by AAA similarity.
answer.worked:
$\angle BAX=\angle EDY$, since $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ and the altitude feet lie on the corresponding bases.

$\angle AXB=\angle DYE=90^\circ$, since $BX$ and $EY$ are altitudes.

The third pair of angles is also equal, so $\triangle ABX\sim\triangle DEY$ by AAA similarity.

answer.short:
$\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC)$.

Corresponding bases and altitudes each have scale factor $k$, so each triangle formed by an altitude has area scale factor $k^2$. Add the two areas.
answer.worked:
From part (a), the scale factor between $\triangle ABX$ and $\triangle DEY$ is $\frac{DE}{AB}=k$. Thus $DY=kAX$ and $EY=kBX$.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEY)&=\tfrac12 DY\cdot EY\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEY)&=\tfrac12(kAX)(kBX)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEY)&=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABX).\end{align*}$$
Similarly, $\triangle CBX\sim\triangle FEY$, so
$$\operatorname{area}(\triangle FEY)=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle CBX).$$
Adding the two corresponding areas gives
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEY)+\operatorname{area}(\triangle FEY)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=k^2\bigl(\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABX)+\operatorname{area}(\triangle CBX)\bigr)\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DEF)&=k^2\operatorname{area}(\triangle ABC).\end{align*}$$
